name: Kalaktang Monpa
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

earlier_scan.note: Only sociolinguistic surveys (Abraham et al. 2005/2018) and classification notes (Blench 2012); no phonology/grammar of Kalaktang Monpa found

new_statements.quote: Stress in general is non-distinctive, prosodic, and relatively unpronounced. In both disyllabic and polysyllabic words, stress falls on the first syllable. This also holds for polymorphemic lexemes, such as inflected words with suffixes. There are some exceptions among compound phonemes, for example samtoka [sam'to:ka:] 'otter,' nasbaktang [...] ... stress will be indicated by a stress mark [ ] before the stressed syllable, whenever it is not predictable. Prosodic lengthening of vowels is used by speakers in order to emphasise, primarily on adjectives, adverbs and interjections.
new_statements.citation: Bodt, Tim. 2014. Tshangla phonology and a standard Tshangla orthography. In Thomas Owen-Smith & Nathan W. Hill (eds.), Trans-Himalayan Linguistics: Historical and Descriptive Linguistics of the Himalayan Area, 393-436. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110310832.393
new_statements.locator: p. 422 (sec. on stress/prosody); scope statement pp. 393-394
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and weak; it falls on the first syllable of every word of two or more syllables, including inflected words with suffixes. A few compounds keep stress on a non-initial syllable (e.g. samtoka 'otter' on the second), and these unpredictable cases are marked in the lexicon. Independently, Andvik 2010: 17-18 (Trashigang Tshangla) gives the same rule: 'Without exception stress occurs on the first syllable' of disyllabic lexemes and affixes are unstressed, with stress attracted to a closed syllable in some trisyllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the snippets seen (Andvik 2010: 19-20 notes compounds of disyllable + monosyllable stressed on first and third syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Some compounds (samtoka 'otter', nasbaktang...) with non-initial stress, marked in the lexicon 'whenever it is not predictable'; Andvik: a few disyllables with second-syllable stress (meaktsa 'wife', pheaktsa 'husband', balingmi 'white') and closed-syllable attraction in trisyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexemes incl. inflected words and compounds). Statement is about Tshangla as a whole (Bodt's data are Bhutan varieties per Bodt 2022); the chapter explicitly counts the Tshangla of the 'Dirang and Kalaktang blocks of West Kameng' (p. 393) and 'Southern Monpa... the Tshangla speakers of Kalaktang' (p. 394) within its language, but no Kalaktang-specific stress data are shown. Text seen only as Google Books snippets (page from the preview link pg=PA422), not the full chapter.
new_statements.identity_note: No description of Kalaktang Monpa [kkf] itself exists (Glottolog: 0 descriptive refs; earlier scan agreed). The statement quoted is for Tshangla (tsha1245 / tsj). Bodt 2014 (LTBA survey, opened) treats Kalaktang Monpa as two Tshangla varieties: Metsho Tshangla (Kalaktang/Balemu; 'very close to eastern Dungsam Tshangla' of Bhutan) and Tötsho Tshangla (Domkho/Murshing), the latter 'mutually intelligible with' Metsho and Bhutan Tshangla; Bodt's phonology chapter (pp. 393-394) explicitly includes the Tshangla speakers of Kalaktang in its language, and Grollmann 2020: 9 lists Kalaktang as a Tshangla variety. But the ISO 639-3 split (CR 2006-034) rests on Abraham et al. 2005 (62-71% lexical similarity, 55% RTT with Tshangla), and Bodt's and Andvik's stress data are from Bhutan Tshangla. Treat as a Tshangla-level statement extended to kkf, not a kkf-specific finding.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/tone/phonology. Sec. 4 Table 1 + sec. 5.6: Kalaktang (Khalaktang) Monpa = Metsho Tshangla (Abraham et al. 2005 Balemu/Khalaktang varieties) and Tötsho Tshangla (Domkho variety); 'Metsho Tshangla is very close to eastern Dungsam Tshangla spoken just across the border in Bhutan'; Tötsho variety 'mutually intelligible with' Metsho and Bhutan Tshangla; Phudung variety 'incomprehensible to any other Tshangla speaker'. Names existing descriptions: Chakravarty 1953, Das Gupta 1968 (Dirang), wordlists in Abraham et al. 2005.
